question_text:
A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of episodic bleeding from the nose and gums and one episode of blood in her urine. She was treated with chloramphenicol 1 month ago for Rickettsia rickettsii infection. Her pulse is 130/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 105/70 mm Hg. Examination shows mucosal pallor, scattered petechiae, and ecchymoses on the extremities. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL
Hematocrit 26%
Leukocyte count 900/mm3 (30% neutrophils)
Platelet count 50,000/mm3
The physician recommends a blood transfusion and informs her of the risks and benefits. Which of the following red blood cell preparations will most significantly reduce the risk of transfusion-related cytomegalovirus infection?"?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient has pancytopenia likely due to chloramphenicol-induced bone marrow suppression, leading to anemia, low platelet count, and low leukocyte count. This condition increases her risk of infections, including transfusion-related cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. Leukoreduction is a process that removes leukocytes from blood products, significantly reducing the risk of CMV transmission, as CMV resides in leukocytes. This aligns with standard medical consensus that leukoreduction is the most effective method to reduce CMV risk in transfusions. Other options like warming, washing, irradiation, and centrifugation do not specifically target leukocyte removal to the same extent and are less effective in reducing CMV transmission risk. Therefore, leukoreduction is the recommended red blood cell preparation to minimize CMV infection risk in this patient.
